paragraphs: (2) The unqualified Rabbi Yose is the son of Rabbi Chalafta, as related in Kol Kitvei; Tosafot Yeshanim, end of Yoma, writes likewise. See Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Yose said: ‘An incident concerning my father Chalafta, who went to Rabban Gamliel Berabbi’—a great man, Rabbi’s grandfather, Rashi—‘at Tiberias and found him sitting at Yochanan HaNazuf’s table’; see Rabban Gamliel. He was of Yonadav ben Rekhav’s seed: Bereshit Rabbah, section 98.

(3) He lived in the Land of Israel after the destruction: Tosafot, Beitzah 5a. He did not live in the Temple period: Tosafot, beginning of Arakhin, chapter 8. His father Rabbi Chalafta was in Sepphoris: end of Rosh Hashanah. In Echad Dinei Mamonot: ‘Justice, justice shall you pursue’—follow Rabbi Yose to Sepphoris. In Sanhedrin 19a Rabbi Yose instituted an enactment in Sepphoris. Yuchasin, sequence of generations, writes: ‘I am astonished at Bammeh Madlikin 33b, where the king decreed that Rabbi Yose should be exiled to Sepphoris, for he and his fathers were in Sepphoris.’ My difficulty is that the king decreed exile to Sepphoris, yet Bava Metzia 84a, beginning, says Elijah told Rabbi Yishmael be-Rabbi Yose: ‘Your father fled to Asya; flee to Laodicea’; see there. Bereshit Rabbah, Lekh Lekha, end of section 44: Asya is not in the Land of Israel. Arukh says the Targum for Ashkenaz is Asya. Laodicea too is outside the Land; see Pappos and Lulianus above. Were I not afraid, I would say it should read ‘exiled from Sepphoris.’ One should ask why the king specified to which place he should be exiled. Moreover, Sepphoris’s air is pleasant; see Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. Would he flee to a beautiful place? That is no exile; rather, he should be exiled to another country. Understand this. But it is difficult, for he died in Sepphoris. Chelek 109a: when Rabbi Yose departed, Sepphoris’s gutters flowed with blood. Perhaps he returned to Sepphoris when the king died. Or perhaps: there in Chelek, Rabbi Yose expounded at Sepphoris, ‘They break into houses in darkness,’ and so forth, concerning depositing balsam, and so forth; that night three hundred tunnels were dug in Sepphoris, and so forth. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Maaser Sheni’s final chapter, and Bereshit Rabbah, section 27, 30b, end, Rabbi Chanina expounded at Sepphoris, ‘They break into houses in darkness,’ and three hundred houses were broken into. ‘When Rabbi Yose departed, the gutters flowed,’ and so forth. Rashi explains that he was a great man: since it had just mentioned break-ins in Sepphoris, Rabbi Yose’s locality, it also mentioned his departure, to teach that he came from Sepphoris. End quotation. Beer Sheva asks: did we not know until now that Rabbi Yose came from Sepphoris? Rather, this teaches that Heaven showed Sepphoris’s people that he had not sinned in expounding ‘They break into houses in darkness,’ thereby causing three hundred houses to be broken into. End quotation. Perhaps Rashi meant: Rabbi Yose was exiled to Asya and presumably died there; why then did Sepphoris’s gutters pour blood? Therefore he wrote that it teaches he came from Sepphoris: since it had been his home before his exile, his death left a mark there. Understand this. Kirah 38a, end: Rabbi Chanina said, ‘When Rabbi Yose went to Sepphoris, he saw,’ and so forth. This implies Sepphoris was not his home. Perhaps he settled there then.

(4) He composed the unqualified Seder Olam: Yevamot 82b and Niddah 46b. He was very pious. Kol Kitvei 118b: he never looked at his circumcision; his house’s beams never saw his garment’s hem; he never transgressed a colleague’s wish. If they told him to ascend the platform, although he was no priest, he would ascend. He never said anything and turned back from it: Arakhin 15b. He said: ‘May my portion be among those who eat three meals on the Sabbath, complete Hallel every day, pray at the sun’s dimming, die of bowel disease or while engaged in a commandment, bring in the Sabbath at Tiberias, which is low, and bring it out at Sepphoris, which sits on a mountain; those who gather students for study, rather than those who dismiss them for the meal; collectors of charity, rather than distributors of charity; and those who are suspected of something they have not done.’ Elijah regularly came to him. Berakhot 3a: he prayed in a ruin, and Elijah waited until he finished; he learned three things from Elijah. Yevamot, chapter 2—it should read chapter 6—63a: he asked Elijah, ‘I shall make him a helpmate: how does she help him?’ In Chelek 113b Rabbi Yose expounded at Sepphoris: ‘Father Elijah is irascible.’ He did not come to him for three days. After three days Elijah came, and Rabbi Yose asked: ‘Why did Elijah not come?’ He replied: ‘Because he called him irascible.’ Rabbi Yose told him: ‘But the master has taken offense!’ In the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Kol HaTzelamim, when Rabbi Yose bar Chalafta died, pipes drew blood in Laodicea. This requires examination, for he did not die in Laodicea. It was because he risked his life over the decree. Moed Katan 25b: Sepphoris’s gutters poured blood. Tosafot write that he risked his life for sanctifying God’s name. Another explanation: he risked his life over circumcision.

(5) In his days there were no olives in the Land of Israel, because Hadrian had devastated the Land and all the olives: Jerusalem Talmud, Peah, beginning of chapter 7. He tanned hides. Bammeh Tomnin 49a, end: Rabbi Yishmael be-Rabbi Yose said, ‘My father was a tanner,’ and he said to bring hides to the study house to sit upon. His wife used to quarrel with his maid: Bereshit Rabbah, section 48. A matron questioned him: Bereshit Rabbah, sections 17, 25, 63, 68, 87; Shemot Rabbah, chapter 3; Bamidbar Rabbah, chapter 3; Kohelet.

(6) He said: ‘I performed five acts of intercourse’—he would have intercourse and repeat it so that he would have male children—‘and planted five cedars’: Shabbat 118b. Tosafot write: the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 1, says they were widows subject to levirate marriage. He did not wish to fulfill the conjugal obligation with them, but only the commandment of levirate marriage, namely the first intercourse. End quotation. So too Bereshit Rabbah, section 85: he took his brother’s wife in levirate marriage and performed five acts of intercourse. Mattenot Kehunah explains that five levirate widows fell before him. He had intercourse through a sheet so as not to derive pleasure. These were the five plantings: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yishmael—the Gemara puts Rabbi Yishmael before Rabbi Eliezer—Rabbi Chalafta ben Avtolos [as transmitted; perhaps two names, Chalafta and Avtolos, to complete the stated five]; in the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Yevamot, halakhah 1, and Bereshit Rabbah cited above, Rabbi Avrimos; and Rabbi Menachem. Rabbah and the Jerusalem Talmud put the latter before Rabbi Chalafta. Gilgulei Neshamot, letter mem, writes: Machlah, Choglah, Noah, Milkah, and Tirtzah, Tzelofchad’s daughters, spoke at the moment Moses expounded the levirate passage, as in Yalkut, Yehoshua: ‘Let our mother enter levirate marriage.’ They merited to become embodied likewise in pious and wise men, through that righteous man who had intercourse through a sheet; they bore him five sons. His son Chalafta died in his lifetime; nevertheless, he expounded all day through an interpreter: Semachot, chapter 10. I shall show you that he erred: on the contrary, doing it through an interpreter is forbidden. Moed Katan 21a: it is forbidden to read Torah; if many need him, he does not refrain. An incident: Rabbi Yose’s son died at Sepphoris—it does not mention Chalafta—and he entered the study house and expounded the entire day. Rabbah bar bar Chana suffered a bereavement and thought not to go out to the discourse. Rabbi Chanina told him: ‘If many need him, it is permitted.’ He thought to set an expositor over him; Rav told him: ‘Provided he does not appoint an interpreter.’ How, then, should he act? As when Rabbi Yehudah’s son died: he entered the study house, and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya entered and sat beside him. He whispered to Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya; Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya to the interpreter; the interpreter made it heard to the many. End quotation. Semachot, chapter 10, has: ‘Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s son died, and he gave another permission to speak on his behalf.’ End quotation. It does not mention Rabbi Yose’s son or Rabbi Chalafta there, but Rabbi Yose HaGelili.

(7) Rabbi Meir died before him, and he died before Rabbi Yehudah, as related in Sukkah, chapter 1, and Rosh Hashanah, chapter 1; see there. Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin, HaOmer: Rabbi said, ‘As the difference between the holiest sacred things and utterly ordinary things, so is the difference between our generation and Rabbi Yose’s generation.’ Rabbi Yishmael says: ‘As between gold and dust, so between our generation and my father’s generation.’ He was Rabbenu HaKadosh’s teacher. Tinoket 68b: Rabbi asked Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon. There, 53a: Rabbi said, ‘I heard from Rabbi Yose.’ Niddah 14b: Rabbi Yishmael be-Rabbi Yose told Rabbi Chama bar Bisna, ‘He abandons the teacher’s words’—Rabbi Yose—‘and listens to the student’s words’—Rabbi. Tosafot write: Rabbenu Tam explains that at first Rabbi Yose was greater than Rabbi, but afterwards Rabbi grew wiser—through students, so in the new Talmud edition. So too Tosafot, Bammeh Tomnin 51a. Rashi, Sanhedrin 24a, explains that had Rabbi Yose been alive, he would have submitted to Rabbi because of the presidency. There in Sanhedrin, Rabbi said of him: ‘The elder has already ruled.’ So too Yevamot 105b; see Rabbi Yishmael be-Rabbi Yose above. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel told Rabbi Yose Berabbi: Rashbam explains that this is what he called Rabbi Yose bar Chalafta, meaning the generation’s great man, Arvei Pesachim 100a. Tosefta, Zevachim, chapter 1: Rabbi Shimon said, ‘Yose Berabbi found me in Sidon and told me: The carrying which Rabbi Meir invalidated,’ and so forth. Tosefta, Sukkah, chapter 2: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said, ‘Once I suffered in my eyes at Caesarea, and Rabbi Yose Berabbi permitted it.’ Rashi, Sukkah 26a, explains: Yose the sage, the sharp scholar of his generation, Rabbi Yose bar Chalafta. Tosefta, Berakhot, chapter 5: Rabban Gamliel—Pesachim above has Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel—told Rabbi Yose, and so forth. Rabbi Yose replied: ‘Every day you favor my words before Rabbi Yehudah, and now you favor Rabbi Yehudah’s words! Will you even subdue the queen?’ and so forth. Megalleh Amukkot 191 writes: Rabbi Yose draws sustenance from the name Elohim, whose numerical value is Yose, as in Raaya Mehemna, Pinchas, at the locator עת״י. Therefore the law follows him in ninety-five places in the Talmud, the numerical value of malkah, queen. Hence ‘Will you even subdue the queen in the house?’ Its mystery is the raw letter groups ה״צ ו״פ. That is, since he draws sustenance from the name Elohim, totaling eighty-six, the law follows him ninety-five times; see there.

(8) Rabbi Akiva was his teacher. Pesachim 18a–b: Rabbi Yose said it according to Rabbi Akiva his teacher’s position. So too Arukh, entry kara: Rabbi Yose was Rabbi Akiva’s student; see there. His colleagues were Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yehudah, and Rabbi Meir. Tosafot, Yoma 8a, likewise calls Rabbi Meir his colleague and disputant. He praised him; see his entry. And Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua; see above, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. He traveled with Rabbi Yehudah and was seized by ravenous hunger: Yoma 83b.

(9) (a) The law follows him everywhere in the Mishnah and baraita against his colleagues, because his reasoning is with him, as in Mi SheHotziuhu 51a. See Rashi there: nim kav, a matter straight as a plumb line. Tosafot, Eruvin 83b and Bava Kamma 24a: his reasons and proofs; Eruvin 14b; Gittin 67a: all his teaching is clear; Tosafot, Taanit 28a. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes: this is puzzling regarding Tosafot Yom Tov, Maaser Sheni 5:2 and end of Terumot. (b) Rabbi Nechemyah and Rabbi Yose, and likewise Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Yose: the law follows Rabbi Yose. Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3. (c) Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yose: the law follows Rabbi Yose, Beitzah 31a. They did not rely on the general rule that the law follows Rabbi Yose against Rabbi Yehudah, because Rabbi Yehudah’s words were reasonable; he therefore needed to rule according to Rabbi Yose (Responsa Nachalah LiYehoshua). See Responsa Chavvot Yair 47a, end of Yevamot, chapter 8, Tosafot, Kiddushin 79b, Rosh Hashanah 33a, and Moed Katan 17b, end, 26b. (d) Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose: the law follows Rabbi Yose, Sanhedrin 27a, even regarding Rabbi Meir’s decrees; see Responsa Chavvot Yair. Rosh, end of Avodah Zarah, chapter 1: ‘Rav Yehudah said: Shmuel said, the law follows Rabbi Meir’ should read ‘the law follows Rabbi Yose,’ as in the Gemara, Rif, and the abridgment of Rosh’s decisions. So too Beer Sheva, beginning of Horayot. (e) Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yose: the law follows Rabbi Yose, Eruvin 46b. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes: I find it difficult—why did Rav Nachman need to say in Bava Kamma, ‘I hold like Rabbi Yose,’ when everyone holds like Rabbi Yose against Rabbi Shimon? I found written: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yose, the law follows Rabbi Yose.

(10) Avtolmos was his teacher. Isi ben Yehudah was his student; see Isi ben Akiva. Rabbi Elazar Deroma asked before him. He testified in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s name: Tosefta, Shabbat, chapter 15. Abba Elazar spoke to him. Rabbi Yose says in Rabban Gamliel’s name: anyone who has a craft resembles a woman with a husband, and so forth. Another reading: anyone without a craft resembles a woman without a husband. Tosefta, Kiddushin, chapter 1; see Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Elazar above. Rav Huna transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yose said: ‘Sometimes I ate with Rabbi Chalafta my father and Rabbi Chanina bar Susi’—Tosafot in the Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 48a, has Sarsu—‘my beloved,’ meaning his uncle. They did not count him in the invitation to grace until he grew two hairs. Jerusalem Talmud, Sheloshah SheAkhelu, mishnah 2; Rabbah, Mikketz, section 91. Rabbi Chanina said: ‘When Rabbi Yose went to Sepphoris’; see above. Rabbi Chananyah the deputy high priest disputes with him. Chananyah of Ono disputes with him. Rabbi Yehudah said: ‘We used to eat lof after the festival on Rabbi Tarfon’s authority.’ Rabbi Yose told him: ‘I was with you, and it was after Passover’: Tosefta, Sheviit, chapter 4. Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava ordained him. Yehudah of Hutzal asked him. Rabbi Yehudah ben Agra transmitted in his name. In Rabbi Yehoshua’s name: Arvei Pesachim 103a. Rabbi Yochanan transmitted in his name. An incident came before Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: Tosefta, Sheviit, chapter 4. In Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri’s name: Tosefta, Kelim, chapter 2 and end of the final chapter. He said: ‘Yonatan ben Charsha asked at Yavneh.’ Rabbi Yaakov bar Avina transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yose addressed Rabbi Meir. See Shir HaShirim Rabbah, on ‘Sustain me with raisin cakes.’ Nimos conversed with him. Rabbi Simon in Rabbi Yose’s name, in Rabbi Nehoraya’s name. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri was his colleague. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah of Akko transmitted in his name. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel transmitted in his name: Avodah Zarah 75a and Niddah 65b. He permitted Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel to sleep outside the sukkah. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah transmitted in his name: Makkot 20a.
